6.1.l: Pediatric Hip — Perthes Disease: Treatment & Prognosis
6.1.b:
Treatment depends first on one question: is the disease still active, or already healed?

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you treat Perthes?"
- "First I ask: **active** disease, or a **healed** hip with residual deformity?"
- "Active: keep the head **spherical** by motion and **containment**."
- "Healed: correct only a deformity that causes the **patient** a problem."

### Active Versus Healed Disease
The two phases need opposite thinking.
[[FIG: Fig 6.1 · 6.1

| | Active disease | Healed disease |
|---|---|---|
| Marker | not yet healed | **subchondral ossification** |
| Head | plastic, mouldable | final shape, no longer mouldable |
| Aim | keep sphericity; reduce deforming stress | relieve the patient's problem |
| Treatment | **head containment** | **correction of residual deformity** |

- **Subchondral ossification** is the hallmark of healing (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
[[FIG: Fig 6.2 · 6.1
- After it appears, no treatment can change the head shape
- Stages and their films → 05 Perthes Pathology

#### Biological Plasticity
- The active head is soft and **deformable**
[[FIG: Fig 6.3 · 6.1
- The acetabulum is its mould: round mould, round head
- Salter called this **biological plasticity**

PITFALL — Perthes on the film is not active Perthes
- A 9-year-old whose disease began at 5 often arrives already **healed**
- Containment surgery for that hip only adds risk
- Say → "**Containment works only before subchondral ossification; a healed head is treated for symptoms**"

### Phases of Management
The Handbook splits treatment by stage.

| Phase | Timing | Aim |
|---|---|---|
| **Initial** (symptomatic) | before head deformity | relieve pain, restore motion |
| **Reconstructive** | fragmentation to end of reossification | keep the head contained and spherical |
| **Remodelling** | head fully ossified | observe until maturity |
| **Salvage** | deformity already present | reduce pain and functional loss |

- Fragmentation itself is wanted: it clears dead bone, so do not try to stop it
- Head-at-risk signs matter only for the reconstructive phase

### Aims of Treatment
Three aims, in this order (Miller).
- **Relieve symptoms**: rest, anti-inflammatory drugs, crutches, short traction
- **Restore range of motion**: the most important single measure
- **Contain** the head: the acetabulum moulds it while it heals
- Neither osteotomy speeds the healing of the disease

MEMORY HOOK — the jelly in the mould
- Perthes is jelly setting in a mould: keep the jelly moving inside a round mould until it sets, and it sets round. Once set, no mould will reshape it.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what decides the prognosis?"
- "Two strong factors: **age at onset** and the **lateral pillar** group."
- "Then **motion**, **subluxation** and **sex**; extent of necrosis matters little."
- "Final outcome is graded by **Stulberg**, which predicts arthritis."

### Age at Onset
Age is the strongest single factor.
- Young children have thick cartilage around a small **ossific nucleus**
- The cartilage keeps the head round even if the nucleus breaks
- Older children have thin cartilage, so the nucleus collapse shows in the head
- A young boy may heal round with no treatment at all
[[FIG: Fig 6.4 · 6.2

MEMORY HOOK — the egg in the silicone ball
- Drop a bare egg and it cracks; drop it inside a thick silicone ball and it survives. The young child's head is the egg in a thick ball of cartilage.

#### Which Age Counts
- Use the age at **onset**, not the age today
- A 9-year-old with 3 years of symptoms had onset at **6**
- The cut-off is **8 years** chronological, about **6 years** skeletal (Miller)
- Perthes children have **delayed bone age**, hence the two numbers

### Prognostic Factors
A large study weighed every factor against the final Stulberg class.
[[FIG: Fig 6.5 · 6.2

| Factor | Weight (Prof Abdel-Ghani) |
|---|---|
| **Age at onset** | strongest |
| **Lateral pillar group** | strongest |
| Lateral calcification | strong |
| **Subluxation** | strong |
| **Mobility** (range of motion) | strong |
| **Sex** | strong |
| Extent of necrosis | weak |
| Metaphyseal involvement | weak |
| Gage sign · horizontal physis | none |

- **Girls** do worse: they mature earlier, so less time to remodel
- Skeletal maturity: girls ≈**14** years, boys ≈**16** (Miller)
- **Obesity** and lost **abduction** also predict a poor result
- Extent of necrosis predicts poorly: Catterall III can do worse than IV
- Head-at-risk signs and their films → 05 Perthes Pathology

#### Motion
- The head must move inside the socket for the mould to work
- Lost motion leaves the head under the acetabular edge
- The edge bites the lateral head → **mushroom** deformity
- Loss of motion at any time means the prognosis has changed

#### Lateral Extrusion
| Measure | Poor prognosis (Handbook) |
|---|---|
| Lateral **centre–edge angle** | under **20°** (normal 20–40°) |
| **Extrusion index** | over **20%** of the head width |

- Subluxation = a broken **Shenton line**: true collapse of the head

### Prognosis by Lateral Pillar and Age
Herring's study links group and age to the chance of a spherical head.
[[FIG: Fig 6.6 · 6.2

| Group | Early onset (under eight) | Late onset (over eight) |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Stulberg I–II at all ages | Stulberg I–II at all ages |
| **B** | **70–90%** Stulberg I–II | 50–70% Stulberg I–II |
| **B/C** | ≈50% Stulberg I–II | almost none |
| **C** | under 20% | almost none |

- Before 8 years, Stulberg IV–V is rare in any group
[[FIG: Fig 6.7 · 6.2
- After 8, IV–V rises in B, and sharply in B/C and C
- Group C with onset near **11 years** ends almost always IV–V
- Herring C does badly at all ages, whatever the treatment (Campbell)

#### Limits of Prediction
- These are percentages for a group, not a forecast for one child
- A poor prognosis alone does not justify surgery
- Surgery must be shown to **change the natural history**

### Early Prediction
The lateral pillar can be graded only well into fragmentation.
- That wait takes **4–6 months** (Campbell)
- **Perfusion MRI** shows lateral pillar involvement earlier → 05 Perthes Pathology
- About **50%** of children need sedation for it
- It is promising, but not yet standard

Stulberg grades the healed hip and predicts arthritis; it is the yardstick for every treatment.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is the Stulberg classification?"
- "Five classes of the **healed** hip, by head shape and congruity."
- "**I–II spherical**, **III oval**, **IV aspherical congruent**, **V aspherical incongruent**."
- "I–II: no arthritis; V: severe arthritis before **50**."

### Stulberg Classes
Stulberg (**1981**) grouped healed hips by sphericity and fit.

| Class | Head and acetabulum (Campbell) | Group |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | normal, congruent hip | spherical congruence |
| **II** | spherical head, larger (coxa magna), short neck or steep acetabulum | spherical congruence |
| **III** | ovoid, mushroom or umbrella head; not flat | aspherical congruence |
| **IV** | flat head with flat, matching acetabulum | aspherical congruence |
| **V** | flat head, normal neck and acetabulum | aspherical incongruence |

#### Each Class on the Film
- **Class I**: healed head, the same size as the other side
[[FIG: Fig 6.8 · 6.3
- **Class II**: round on AP and frog views, but larger
[[FIG: Fig 6.9 · 6.3
- **Class III**: round contour with no flat part, but AP and frog diameters differ
[[FIG: Fig 6.10 · 6.3
- **Class IV**: a flattened head with a matching, two-curved acetabulum
[[FIG: Fig 6.11 · 6.3
- A mushroom head with no flat segment stays **class III** (Campbell)
- A notch in the head copied by the acetabulum is also **class IV**
[[FIG: Fig 6.12 · 6.3
- Bilateral flat heads with moulded sockets: still class IV
[[FIG: Fig 6.13 · 6.3
- **Class V**: a flat head in a round acetabulum
[[FIG: Fig 6.14 · 6.3

PITFALL — congruent or incongruent?
- "Congruent incongruity" confuses examiners; use sphericity words
- Say → "**Class IV is aspherical congruence; class V is aspherical incongruence**"

#### Congruity and Age
- Congruity matters more than shape: a deformed congruent hip lasts longer
- A **young** acetabulum grows and moulds to the head: congruent
- An **older** acetabulum cannot follow, so it stays round: incongruent
- Worst of all: a deformed head in a completely normal socket

#### When to Apply It
- The old rule waited for skeletal maturity; this is no longer held
- Once subchondral ossification appears, the shape is final
- So Stulberg can be applied as soon as the hip heals

### Natural History
Most children do well for decades; the head shape decides the late result.
[[FIG: Fig 6.15 · 6.3

| Stulberg | Joint narrowing at forty-year follow-up (Prof Abdel-Ghani) |
|---|---|
| **I–II** | **0%** |
| **III** | ≈**47%** |
| **IV** | ≈**53%** |
| **V** | ≈**61%**; severe arthritis before 50 years |

- Most patients do well until the **fifth or sixth decade** (Orthobullets)
- About **half** of aspherical heads develop early osteoarthritis
- Overall, ≈**60%** never need an operation
- Bilateral disease does worse: **48%** end Stulberg IV–V (Campbell)

MEMORY HOOK — round, egg, flat
- A ball lasts (I–II), an egg wobbles (III–IV), and a flat tyre in a round wheel arch wears out first (V).

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is conservative treatment?"
- "Symptomatic care, then **full range of motion** kept by home exercises."
- "Avoid impact: no ball games or jumping; swimming is allowed."
- "Prolonged **bracing** is abandoned: not effective, possibly harmful."

### Initial Stage
In the initial stage, treat symptoms only.
- No pain, good motion: **no intervention**
- Painful or stiff: rest, **anti-inflammatory drugs**, crutches
- Refractory pain: short **skin traction**
- Children **2–3 years** old can simply be observed

#### Core Decompression
- **Not recommended** in the initial stage
- Revascularisation happens anyway after fragmentation
- So drilling the head adds nothing to healing

### Range of Motion
Motion keeps the mould working; it is the most important task.
- Parents do the exercises at home, **2–3 times** a day, ≈15 minutes each
- Passive and active exercises, with **abduction** of both hips together
- Abducting one hip only lets the pelvis tilt: no true abduction
- Physiotherapy machines (heat, vibration, pulses) are useless

#### When Motion Is Lost
- Anti-inflammatory drugs first, to ease pain and spasm
- Still stiff: **adductor tenotomy**, or **Botox** into the adductors
- Campbell adds closed reduction under anaesthesia and an abduction cast
- A short **cast** for 2–3 weeks is used by some

### Activity
Repeated infarctions are mechanical, so protect the head from impact.
- The first infarction is biological; later ones follow **trauma**
- No **ball games**, jumping or falls; no contact sports
- **Swimming** is allowed, and cycling usually
- Do not ban all movement: redirect the child to safe activities

### Bracing and Casting
Containment without surgery was the old standard.
- **Petrie cast**: two long-leg casts joined by a bar, hips abducted and internally rotated
- Abduction orthoses aimed the same at the walking child
- The **Handbook** also lists spica, broomstick cast and abduction brace

#### Why Bracing Was Abandoned
- Large prospective study: no benefit from bracing (Orthobullets)
- Months in a cast cause severe **osteopenia**, which favours collapse
- The disease runs about **2 years**: too long to keep a child braced
- Campbell still uses a Petrie cast for **6 weeks** after adductor tenotomy

### Drugs
- **Bisphosphonates**: no agreed dose, duration or proven effect
- Bone marrow or stem cell injection: **no evidence**

MEMORY HOOK — swim, do not jump
- The Perthes child is a fish, not a kangaroo: swimming and cycling yes, jumping and football no.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which child needs containment surgery?"
- "**Herring B or B/C**, onset after **8 years** (bone age 6)."
- "Active disease, full motion, and a **containable** head: no true hinge abduction."
- "Options: **femoral varus**, **Salter** or triple pelvic osteotomy, or a **shelf**."

### Containment
The head is held inside the acetabulum until it heals.
- The acetabulum acts as a **mould** and keeps the head round
- A lateralised head loses this and the edge deforms it
- Methods: bring the acetabulum over the head, or the head into the acetabulum
- Operate in **early fragmentation**, before the head deforms

### Prerequisites
| Prerequisite | Why |
|---|---|
| **Active** disease | a healed head cannot be reshaped |
| **Indicated** child | B or B/C, onset after 8 |
| **Full range of motion** | a stiff hip cannot be contained |
| **Containable** head | no true hinge abduction, no aspherical congruity |

### Hinge Abduction
In hinge abduction the head no longer rolls; it pivots on the rim.
- The extruded lateral head catches on the **lateral acetabular edge**
[[FIG: Fig 6.16 · 6.5
- The centre of rotation moves from the head centre to that edge
- On abduction the head levers out: the **medial joint space widens**
- Such a head is **uncontainable**

#### True or False Hinge Abduction
- A deformed head may look hinged on the plain film
- Diagnose it by **examination under anaesthesia** with abduction
[[FIG: Fig 6.17 · 6.5
- **Arthrography** in abduction shows medial dye pooling and the hinge
[[FIG: Fig 6.18 · 6.5
- Reducible, the prominent part slides in: false hinge, containable
[[FIG: Fig 6.19 · 6.5

| | True hinge abduction | False hinge abduction |
|---|---|---|
| Extrusion | **not reducible** | reducible |
| Arthrogram in abduction | medial pooling; head levers out | head slides in |
| Head | uncontainable | containable if active |

#### Aspherical Congruity
- A deformed head matched by a moulded acetabulum is congruent
- Moving the head now creates **incongruity** and stiffness
- So aspherical congruity is a second contraindication to containment

PITFALL — limited abduction is not adductor contracture
- In Perthes, limited abduction is usually **pain and spasm**, not a short adductor
- Say → "**Examine under anaesthesia: full abduction means no contracture; a lever on the rim means true hinge abduction**"

### Femoral Varus Osteotomy
Varus turns the head so its lateral part goes inside the acetabulum.
- It protects the **lateral pillar**, the part that matters most
[[FIG: Fig 6.20 · 6.5
- Campbell aims for **0–15°** of varus: more is not better
- Usually with derotation: a **varus derotational osteotomy**
[[FIG: Fig 6.21 · 6.5
- Fixed with a pediatric hip screw and plate, near the lesser trochanter
[[FIG: Fig 6.22 · 6.5

#### Indications (Campbell)
- Child **8–10 years**, without leg-length inequality
- Arthrogram or MRI: head contained in abduction and internal rotation
- Marked femoral **anteversion**, corrected in the same cut

#### Disadvantages
| Drawback | Result |
|---|---|
